The aim of this study is to assess endothelial progenitor cells (EPCs) and circulating endothelial cells (CECs) at the time of type 1 diabetes (T1D) recognition concerning patients’ clinical state, remaining insulin secretion, and further partial remission (PR) occurrence. We recruited 45 children that were admitted to hospital due to newly diagnosed T1D (median age 10.8 yrs), and 20 healthy peers as a control group. EPC and CEC levels were measured at disease onset in PBMC isolated from whole peripheral blood with the use of flow cytometry. Clinical data regarding patients’ condition, C-peptide secretion, and further PR prevalence were analyzed. T1D-diagnosed patients presented higher EPC levels than the control group ( p = 0.026), while no statistical differences in CEC levels and EPC/CEC ratio were observed. Considering only T1D patients, those with better clinical conditions presented lower EPCs ( p = 0.021) and lower EPC/CEC ratios ( p = 0.0002). Patients with C-peptide secretion within a normal range at disease onset presented lower EPC/CEC ratios ( p = 0.027). Higher levels of EPCs were observed more frequently in patients with higher glucose, decreased fasting C-peptide, and lower stimulated C-peptide (all p < 0.05). The presence of DKA was related to higher EPC/CEC ratios ( p = 0.034). Significantly higher levels of CECs were observed in patients who presented partial remission of the disease at 6 months after diagnosis ( p = 0.03) only. In the study group, positive correlations of CECs with age, BMI at onset, and BMI in following years were observed. EPC/CEC ratios correlated positively with glucose levels at hospital admission and negatively with age, BMI, pH, and stimulated C-peptide level. We reveal a new potential for the application of EPCs and CECs as biomarkers, reflecting both endothelial injury and reconstruction processes in children with T1D. There is a need for further research in order to reduce cardiovascular risk in children with T1D. type 1 diabetes children endothelial function vascular complications This research received no external funding. 1. Introduction The fact that individuals affected by type 1 diabetes (T1D) are predisposed to significantly elevated risks of mortality, primarily from cardiovascular diseases (CVD) [ 1 ], is widely acknowledged. It has been proven that even young people with T1D exhibit subclinical vascular damage [ 2 ]. Endothelial abnormalities of both small and large blood vessels induced by diabetes are already present even before the onset of overt clinical microvascular or macrovascular complications, which may indicate that endothelial dysfunction serves as an early indicator of cardiovascular risk [ 3 ]. Diabetes, by promoting oxidative stress, chronic inflammation, and reduced nitric oxide production, contributes to impaired endothelial function [ 4 , 5 ]. Furthermore, chronic hyperglycemia and glucose variability are recognized as being key contributors to endothelial dysfunction in individuals with diabetes [ 6 , 7 , 8 ]. Ongoing research in this area has provided evidence that people with long-lasting type 1 diabetes exhibit a decrease in circulating endothelial progenitor cells (EPCs) compared to those who experience a shorter duration of the disease [ 9 ]. Moreover, patients with diabetes type 1 present increased circulating endothelial cell (CEC) levels than healthy individuals [ 10 ]. This is a significant finding, as EPCs are produced in bone marrow and contribute to neovascularization and the rebuilding of a damaged endothelium, and their reduced number and activity is proven to be connected to greater incidence of both micro- and macrovascular complications of diabetes [ 8 ]. Under exposure to ischemia or hypoxia, hypoxia-induced factor 1 (HIF-1) is activated, which, in turn, enhances the production and release of stromal-derived factor 1 (SDF-1)—a crucial factor that mobilizes EPCs to repair damaged the endothelium [ 11 ]. It has been previously demonstrated that diabetes, regardless of its type, significantly reduces the recruitment of EPCs from bone marrow into peripheral circulation, impairs their function, and increases apoptosis of these cells [ 12 ]. On the other hand, CECs (cells of the exfoliated endothelium) are secreted into the bloodstream during vascular injury; thus, they can serve as a marker of ongoing endothelial damage [ 13 , 14 ]. The characteristics of the above-mentioned cells and endothelium function at type 1 diabetes diagnosis are currently poorly described, especially in the youngest group of newly diagnosed patients. These patients have the greatest potential to minimize the risk of long-term complications, as long as actions aimed at achieving optimal glycemic control are introduced in the initial phase of the disease [ 15 ]. It has been demonstrated that early and effective glycemic control among T1D individuals is associated with the longer preservation of pancreatic beta cell function and, consequently, higher C-peptide levels [ 16 ]. Noteworthy, C-peptide serves not only as a marker of endogenous insulin production, but also acts as an active biological agent with antioxidant, anti-apoptotic, and anti-inflammatory properties [ 17 ]. Research indicates that patients diagnosed with type 1 diabetes who have detectable C-peptide levels tend to develop fewer microvascular complications than those without, potentially due to reduced endothelial injury [ 18 ]. This association could be explained by the protective effects of C-peptide on the endothelium [ 18 , 19 ]. The early stage of diabetes diagnosis appears to be a critical point in the disease course. This highlights the need to maintain optimal glycemic control and prolong the duration of partial remission for as long as possible, as this decreases the risk of subsequent diabetes-related complications, as well as enables us to identify biomarkers that can predict the risk of negative vascular outcomes later in life. Taking the above factors into consideration, we evaluated EPC and CEC levels at T1D diagnosis considering patients’ clinical conditions, residual insulin secretion, and the occurrence of partial remission. Our aim was to evaluate EPCs and CECs’ potential as indicators of early endothelial injury and predictors of vascular consequences in the future. We also attempted to identify the mechanisms underlying the observed relationships that may also play a role in developing novel therapies designed to lower cardiovascular risk in T1D patients.

molecular_mechanism_and_relationship.activity_type_context: Endothelial dysfunction and damage in Type 1 Diabetes (T1D), particularly at disease onset, and the role of C-peptide in endothelial function.
molecular_mechanism_and_relationship.mechanism_description: EPCs are bone marrow-derived cells essential for neovascularization and repair of damaged endothelium; their reduced number and activity are linked to vascular complications in T1D, as diabetes impairs their function and recruitment. Elevated EPCs in newly diagnosed T1D likely represent an early compensatory response to subclinical endothelial damage. CECs are exfoliated endothelial cells released during vascular injury, serving as markers of ongoing endothelial damage. C-peptide, a marker of endogenous insulin, is also an active biological agent with antioxidant, anti-apoptotic, and anti-inflammatory properties that positively affect endothelial function by improving nitric oxide production and reducing oxidative stress; lowered C-peptide levels can lead to adverse endothelial effects.

dose_intensity_and_specificity.dose_comparison_summary: Higher EPC levels and EPC/CEC ratios are associated with worse clinical conditions in T1D, including higher glucose, lower fasting and stimulated C-peptide, and the presence of Diabetic Ketoacidosis (DKA). Conversely, patients with better clinical conditions, normal C-peptide secretion, or a more benign clinical course presented lower EPCs and EPC/CEC ratios. Higher levels of CECs were observed in patients achieving partial remission of the disease at 6 months post-diagnosis, and correlated positively with age and BMI at onset and in subsequent years. Well-controlled T1D patients showed lower EPCs, while older age at T1D diagnosis and higher BMI were associated with increased CEC levels. Therapeutic interventions such as insulin pump therapy, ACE inhibition, and statin therapy were noted to positively affect EPC amounts and function.
dose_intensity_and_specificity.specificity_finding: Endothelial Progenitor Cells (EPCs) are primarily involved in the reconstruction and repair of the endothelium, while Circulating Endothelial Cells (CECs) serve as direct markers of ongoing endothelial damage. The study highlights that EPC dynamics are significantly influenced by disease progression and glycemic status, with a specific focus on early-phase Type 1 Diabetes (T1D) responses, which may differ from later stages. While no significant difference in CEC levels was observed between newly diagnosed T1D patients and non-diabetic controls, the elevation of CECs in partial remission is interpreted as an active endothelial repair process or enhanced endothelial turnover rather than progressive damage. The EPC/CEC ratio, though potentially reflecting endothelial repair mechanisms, did not significantly differ between young individuals with newly diagnosed T1D and healthy controls, suggesting it may not be a primary marker for initial T1D diagnosis in this specific comparison. Maintained or lower EPC levels in well-controlled T1D patients are associated with a reduced risk of cardiovascular events and improved long-term outcomes.

clinical_implication_and_population.target_population: Children and young individuals (6-18 years old) with newly diagnosed Type 1 Diabetes (T1D), including those with varying clinical conditions, C-peptide secretion levels, and the presence of partial remission. The study also makes comparisons with healthy control peers (9-17.5 years) and references insights from well-controlled T1D patients, long-term T1D patients, and individuals with higher bodyweight or longer-lasting diabetes.
clinical_implication_and_population.health_implication: Endothelial dysfunction is an early indicator of cardiovascular risk and subclinical vascular damage in children and young people with T1D, predisposing them to elevated risks of mortality primarily from cardiovascular diseases. Endothelial Progenitor Cells (EPCs) and Circulating Endothelial Cells (CECs) are potential biomarkers reflecting both endothelial injury and reconstruction processes, crucial for early detection of vascular complications and predicting long-term vascular outcomes. Elevated EPC levels at T1D onset may signal early subclinical endothelial injury and alterations. Higher EPC/CEC ratios are associated with worse clinical conditions and DKA, indicating increased endothelial damage. Conversely, higher CEC levels are significantly associated with partial remission, suggesting active endothelial repair. The study aims to improve understanding of these markers to reduce cardiovascular risk and guide novel therapies aimed at preserving endothelial repairing capacity in T1D patients.
clinical_implication_and_population.risk_classification: Diagnostic Utility: EPCs and CECs serve as potential biomarkers for detecting early endothelial dysfunction and injury in children with newly diagnosed T1D. The EPC/CEC ratio may characterize the dynamic interaction between endothelial regeneration and injury. Adverse Risk: Elevated EPC levels and higher EPC/CEC ratios are indicative of early endothelial injury, worse clinical conditions (e.g., higher glucose, lower C-peptide, presence of DKA), and increased ongoing endothelial damage. Lowered C-peptide levels may lead to adverse endothelial effects, and chronic endothelial damage, particularly in individuals with higher bodyweight or longer-lasting diabetes, increases cardiovascular risk. Protective Benefit: Lower EPC levels in well-controlled T1D patients suggest reduced cardiovascular risk and better long-term outcomes. Higher CEC levels are significantly associated with partial remission, indicating an active endothelial repair process. Preserving endothelial repairing capacity through interventions like promoting EPC expansion, dietary changes, lifestyle modifications, and therapies such as insulin pump, ACE inhibition, and statins, can mitigate cardiovascular risk. C-peptide itself has a protective effect on the endothelium.

biomarker_reliability_and_future_focus.reliability_assessment: EPCs and CECs were measured using validated flow cytometry methods (markers including anti-CD34, anti-CD133, anti-CD144, anti-CD309) on PBMCs from peripheral blood, revealing new potential for their application as biomarkers. However, the study was conducted on a small group at a single center, with noted age and BMI discrepancies between control and study groups. The interpretation of the EPC/CEC ratio remains hypothetical, and its biological significance in pediatric T1D, including the interpretation of CEC elevation in partial remission as an active endothelial repair process, has not yet been definitively established or correlated with the duration of partial remission. EPC dynamics are recognized to be influenced by disease progression and glycemic status.
